q: Which frontage places parking in the first layer and keeps the facade no more than 80 ft from the right-of-way?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Slip Lane requires the facade to be within 80 ft of the right-of-way and puts parking in the first layer.

q: Which pattern is highly responsive to terrain and evenly disperses traffic through a web?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Riverside responds strongly to terrain and disperses traffic through its web.

q: Which zone has shallow setbacks and continuous streetwalls using arcade, shopfront, stoop, and forecourt frontages?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 combines shallow setbacks with continuous streetwalls and those four frontage types.

q: Which wind exposure describes large city centers where at least 50% of buildings exceed 70 ft in height?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure A is for dense city centers where at least half of the buildings are taller than 70 ft. (Exposure A comes from ASCE 7-98; NSCP 2015 uses only Exposures B, C and D.)

q: What synonym is associated with the Riverside pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Riverside is identified with the Olmstedian model.

q: Which zone uses road, residential street, and avenue to create varied streetscape conditions?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 creates varied conditions with roads, residential streets, and avenues.

q: What default applies when a site does not meet the definition of another wind exposure category?
n: Exposure C applies wherever Exposure B or D does not (NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A.7.3, following ASCE 7).

q: Which disadvantage is associated with the Radburn pattern?
o: High number of awkward lot shapes
Traffic congestion from absence of a web
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn can experience traffic congestion because it lacks an interconnected web.

q: In which zone are thoroughfares primarily roads and drives, with some buildings served by rear lanes?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 uses roads and drives as thoroughfares; wider lots may dispense with rear lanes.

q: What maximum general height is given for surface undulations or irregularities in Exposure C terrain?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure C allows scattered terrain irregularities with heights generally less than 30 ft.

q: Which criterion should an urban designer consider first because it involves pedestrian and vehicle circulation through the district as a whole?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Permeability is considered first because it deals with pedestrian and vehicle circulation across the district.

q: Which zone uses streets and boulevards, with every building served by rear alleys?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 uses streets and boulevards and has rear alleys serving all buildings.

q: Which exposure involves flat, unobstructed areas exposed to wind flowing over open water for at least 1 mile?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure D applies to flat, unobstructed terrain where wind comes over open water for at least 1 mile.

q: Which criterion describes spaces that support many uses instead of locking them into one fixed activity?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Robustness refers to building and outdoor spaces that can support multiple purposes and activities.

q: Which zones organize open space as plazas or squares?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 and T6 both organize open space as plazas or squares.

q: How far inland does Exposure D extend from the shoreline at minimum before considering the height-based alternative?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure D extends inland 1,500 ft or 10 times the building height, whichever is greater.

q: Which criterion encourages people to put their own mark on the places where they live and work?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Personalization encourages users to make their own mark on their living and working environments.

q: Which street pattern uses straight lines to enhance rolling terrain?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: The Savannah pattern uses straight lines that work well with rolling terrain.

q: Which street pattern easily absorbs environmental interruptions while remaining responsive to terrain?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn is responsive to terrain and can absorb environmental interruptions easily while maintaining a local and collector street hierarchy.

q: What is usually required for the private use of the right-of-way in a Gallery & Arcade frontage?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: An easement for private use of the right-of-way is usually required for the arcade condition.

q: What is another name for the Savannah pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Savannah is synonymous with the orthogonal grid or gridiron.

q: In which zone does the area vary according to whether the neighborhood is more village-like or town-like?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: The size of T3 varies with whether the neighborhood model is more rural or more urban.

q: Why is residential use generally precluded on the ground floor of a Shopfront & Awning condition?
o: The presence of a deep setback
The lack of an exterior stair
The use of a private alley
The absence of a raised ground story
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: The frontage’s sidewalk-grade ground floor lacks the raised story that would provide residential privacy. Residential use is more appropriate above.

q: Which pattern absorbs environmental interruptions easily and reduces monotony through terminated vistas?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Nantucket is adaptable to environmental interruptions and uses terminated vistas to reduce monotony.

q: Which zone is usually shared by several neighborhoods and functions as the densest business, service, and institutional center?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 is the most dense business, service, and institutional center and may serve several neighborhoods.

q: Which frontage places part of the facade back from a line that otherwise stays close to the frontage line?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: A forecourt keeps most of the facade close to the frontage line while setting a portion back.

q: Which pattern uses diagonals for through traffic and has well-defined diagonal intersections?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Mariemont uses diagonal routes while maintaining an evenly dispersed grid.

q: A large residential catchment within walking distance is most closely associated with which zone?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 is normally within walking distance of a large residential catchment.

q: Where should trees in forecourts be positioned to improve the sidewalk condition?
o: Only at the rear property line
At the center of the roadway
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Trees in forecourts should have canopies that overhang sidewalks for shade and shelter.

q: What are common synonyms for the Mariemont pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Mariemont is associated with the Unwin model and spider web.

q: Which two zones have open land use that encourages combinations of residential and other uses?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: Both T5 and T6 use open land-use patterns that encourage combinations of residential and other uses.

q: What minimum porch width is recommended for a useful Porch & Fence frontage?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: The porch should be at least 8 ft wide to be useful.

q: Which disadvantage of the Washington pattern concerns parcel geometry?
o: High number of awkward lot shapes
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Washington can create a high number of awkwardly shaped lots.

q: Which zone permits higher-density attached courtyard, rearyard, and sideyard building types?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 uses higher-density attached courtyard, rearyard, and sideyard building types.

q: Which frontage is appropriate for higher-speed thoroughfares because the large setback buffers traffic?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: The large setback of a Common Lawn provides a buffer from faster traffic.

q: Which pattern combines deflected vistas with easy absorption of environmental interruptions?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Riverside interrupts monotony through deflected vistas and adapts easily to environmental interruptions.

q: Which zone has variegated frontages with medium setbacks such as dooryard and porch-and-fence?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 uses medium setbacks with dooryard, porch, and fence conditions.

q: What is provided along frontages to connect transit stops directly to the private sidewalk system?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Landscaped sidewalk systems provide shade and shelter, act as a streetwall buffer, and connect transit stops to private sidewalks.

q: Which disadvantage of Riverside concerns roadway organization?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Riverside has no intrinsic hierarchy.

q: Which zone creates the most rural streetscape conditions using parkway, road, and lane?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 uses parkway, road, and lane and produces the most rural streetscape conditions.

q: Which condition is typical of Exposure B?
o: Flat, unobstructed terrain facing open water for a mile or more
Dense city centers where half the buildings exceed 70 ft
Open terrain with scattered obstructions under 30 ft high
Urban, suburban and wooded areas with many close obstructions
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure B covers urban and suburban areas, wooded areas, and similar terrain with numerous closely spaced obstructions.

q: Which pattern offers controllable variety of blocks and lots while responding well to terrain?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn combines controlled variety of blocks and lots with terrain responsiveness.

q: Which zone creates the most urban streetscape conditions with commercial street, avenue, and boulevard?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 has the most urban streetscapes and uses commercial streets, avenues, and boulevards.

q: For Exposure C, how far must open terrain extend from the building site in any quadrant?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure C generally requires open terrain to extend more than 1,500 ft from the building site in any quadrant.

q: Which criterion concerns how design affects where people can and cannot go within a city district?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Permeability concerns the degree to which design allows or restricts movement through the city district.

q: Which zone uses avenues and streets, with all buildings served by rear alleys?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 uses avenues and streets and requires rear alleys for all buildings.

q: Which areas are explicitly included in Exposure C?
o: Open water, the Great Lakes and ocean coastlines
Wooded suburbs with closely spaced single houses
Dense downtowns with many tall office towers
Flat open country, grasslands and hurricane-prone shores
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure C includes flat open country, grasslands, and shorelines in hurricane-prone regions.

q: Which criterion relates to how easily people understand the spatial layout of a place?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Legibility concerns how understandable the spatial arrangement of a place is to its users.

q: Which zone organizes open space as parks and greens?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 organizes open space as parks and greens.

q: Which shorelines are specifically included in Exposure D?
o: Flat open country and grassland with few trees
Hurricane-prone shorelines of the Gulf and Atlantic
Suburban lakes ringed by closely spaced houses
Inland waterways, the Great Lakes and Pacific coasts
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure D includes inland waterways, the Great Lakes, and specified coastal areas of California, Oregon, Washington, and Alaska.

q: Which criterion seeks to expand sensory experiences such as touch, sound, light, and taste?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Richness increases the range of sensory experiences available to users.

q: Which street pattern provides end grain of blocks for fast traffic?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Savannah has end-grain block conditions that support fast traffic movement.

q: Which street pattern provides even dispersal of traffic through a grid while using diagonal routes for through traffic?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Mariemont combines diagonal through routes with even dispersal of traffic through the grid.

q: How wide should a useful arcade be at minimum?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: The arcade should be at least 12 ft wide to be useful.

q: Which disadvantage belongs to the Savannah pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Savannah is unresponsive to steep terrain, and it also tends to be monotonous and poor at absorbing environmental interruptions.

q: Which zone is the least dense and most purely residential part of a neighborhood?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 is the least dense and most purely residential zone. T4 is mixed but mainly residential, while T5 and T6 are progressively more urban.

q: Which frontage is conventional for retail use and may use a cantilevered shed roof or awning?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Shopfront & Awning is a conventional retail frontage and may have a cantilevered shed roof or awning.

q: Which pattern is especially responsive to terrain and follows traces in the landscape?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Nantucket responds to terrain and follows traces in the landscape.

q: Which zone is the dense multifunctional social condenser of a neighborhood?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 is the dense multifunctional social condenser and is generally positioned centrally.

q: Which frontage is suitable for ground-floor residential uses at short setbacks with rowhouses and apartment buildings?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Stoops support ground-floor residential uses at short setbacks and are common with rowhouses and apartments.

q: What synonym is associated with the Nantucket pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: The Nantucket pattern is associated with the Sitte model and townscape.

q: Which zone always straddles thoroughfares at their most active intersection?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 always straddles thoroughfares at their most active intersection.

q: Why should the forecourt type be used sparingly?
o: It cannot hold any planting, seating or drop-off space
A long run of deep setbacks becomes dull and unsafe to walk
It forces the ground floor to be raised above the walk
It is allowed only on corner lots of the urban core
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Excessive continuous setbacks can reduce pedestrian safety and visual interest.

q: Which disadvantage is associated with the Mariemont pattern?
o: It creates a high number of awkward lots
It causes congestion from the absence of a web
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Mariemont tends to be disorienting despite its hierarchy and diagonal organization.

q: Which zone permits a controlled combination of residential and other uses?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 has limited land use but allows a controlled mix of residential and other uses.

q: Which frontage places a facade behind the frontage line but adds an encroaching porch?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Porch & Fence combines a setback facade with a projecting porch and a fence at the frontage line.

q: Which pattern uses diagonal routes to interrupt the monotony of a grid?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Washington uses diagonals to break up an otherwise gridded layout.

q: Which zone uses medium-density freestanding sideyard and edgeyard building types?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 is characterized by medium-density freestanding sideyard and edgeyard buildings.

q: Which frontage is intended to resemble buildings sitting in a shared rural landscape?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Common Lawn simulates buildings placed within a shared rural landscape rather than behind individual fences.

q: Which synonyms are associated with the Washington pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Washington is associated with City Beautiful and the Haussmann model.

q: Which zone has frontages with deep setbacks such as common lawn and porch-and-fence conditions?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 frontages weakly define public space and use deep setbacks, including common lawn and porch-and-fence types.

q: In a Slip Lane frontage, where are private sidewalks located?
o: Between the curb and roadway centerline
Between the public sidewalk and building entrances
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Private sidewalks run between the public sidewalk and the building entrances.

q: Which disadvantage of the Riverside pattern means that movement through it can be confusing?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Riverside is highly disorienting even though it is responsive to terrain.

q: Which zone has the same continuous-streetwall frontage types as T5 but at the most urban density?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 also uses arcade, shopfront, stoop, and forecourt with continuous streetwalls and shallow setbacks.

q: What minimum upwind distance of representative Exposure A terrain is required for Exposure A to apply?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure A requires representative Exposure A terrain upwind for at least 0.5 mile or 10 times the building height, whichever is greater. (Exposure A comes from ASCE 7-98; NSCP 2015 uses only Exposures B, C and D.)

q: Which pattern provides a good street hierarchy for local and collector movement?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn provides a good hierarchy for local streets and collectors.

q: Which zone creates urban streetscapes with residential streets, commercial streets, avenues, and boulevards?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 uses those four street types to create urban conditions.

q: Which terrain description best matches Exposure C?
o: Wooded terrain with closely spaced houses
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure C is open terrain with scattered obstructions and generally low surface irregularities.

q: What is a synonym for the Radburn pattern?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn is associated with cul-de-sac organization.

q: Which zone uses avenues, streets, and roads, with most buildings served by rear lanes?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 uses avenues, streets, and roads, and most buildings are served by rear lanes.

q: When can a building in Exposure B terrain also be classified as Exposure C?
o: When it stands next to a wooded area on one side of the site
When it adjoins qualifying Exposure C terrain for over 600 ft
When it lies within half a mile of a dense city center
When the building itself is taller than 70 ft above grade
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: A building in Exposure B may be treated as Exposure C when it directly adjoins qualifying open Exposure C terrain for more than 600 ft in any quadrant.

q: The range of users supported by housing, shopping, employment, and recreation is called what?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Variety refers to the range of users and activities a place can accommodate, including housing, shopping, jobs, and recreation.

q: Where may open space be provided as parks within a proximate greenbelt?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 may have parks within the nearby greenbelt.

q: What minimum open-water fetch is associated with Exposure D?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Exposure D requires at least 1 mile (1.61 km) of wind exposure over open water.

q: Which criterion concerns how design can make people aware of the choices a place offers?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Visual appropriateness concerns how the physical design makes the available choices apparent to people.

q: Which street pattern provides excellent directional orientation and controllable lot depth?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Savannah provides strong directional orientation and controllable lot depth through its orthogonal grid.

q: For Exposure D, which determines the inland extent when the two criteria differ?
o: The smaller of 1,500 ft or 10 times building height
Exactly 10 times height in every case
The greater of 1,500 ft or 10 times building height
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: The Exposure D inland distance is the greater of 1,500 ft and 10 times the building or structure height.

q: Which frontage type is conventionally used for retail and uses a colonnade that overlaps the sidewalk?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Gallery & Arcade is a retail-oriented private frontage in which a colonnade overlaps the sidewalk.

q: Which street pattern is efficient for double-loading alleys and utilities?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Savannah’s regular grid supports efficient double-loading of alleys and utilities.

q: Which pattern is synonymous with the cul-de-sac?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Radburn is associated with cul-de-sac organization, which separates local residential circulation from a continuous through-traffic web.

q: Which frontage aligns the facade close to the frontage line with the entrance at sidewalk grade?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Shopfront & Awning places the facade close to the frontage line and keeps the entrance at sidewalk grade.

q: Which pattern has a hierarchy with long routes for through traffic and even dispersal through a web?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Nantucket combines a hierarchy of long through routes with an interconnected web that disperses traffic.

q: Which zone is mixed in function but principally residential and usually the largest part of the neighborhood?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T4 is mixed in function but mainly residential and is usually the neighborhood’s largest area.

q: Which frontage elevates the first story above the sidewalk for privacy and uses an exterior stair and landing?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: A stoop raises the first story from the sidewalk and uses an exterior stair and landing at the entrance.

q: Which is a disadvantage of the Nantucket pattern?
o: Uncontrollable variety of blocks and lots
Congestion by absence of a web
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Nantucket’s irregularity can produce uncontrolled variation in blocks and lots.

q: Which zone is usually within walking distance of surrounding primarily residential areas?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T5 is centrally located and normally within walking distance of surrounding residential areas.

q: Which frontage creates space suited to gardens, vehicular drop-offs, and utility off-loading?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Forecourts provide a setback area that can accommodate gardens, drop-offs, and utility off-loading.

q: Which pattern interrupts monotony with deflected vistas and has well-defined diagonal intersections?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Mariemont combines deflected vistas with spatially well-defined diagonal intersections.

q: Which zone has restricted land use that combines residential use with certain other uses?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 has the most restricted land-use mix, combining residential use with selected other uses.

q: Which frontage uses a shallow setback with a front garden or patio and usually a low wall at the frontage line?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: Dooryard & Light Court uses a shallow setback, often with a garden or patio and low frontage wall.

q: Which pattern uses diagonals for through traffic and focuses diagonally on terrain features?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Washington combines diagonal through routes with diagonal focus on terrain features.

q: Which zone uses low-density freestanding edgeyard buildings?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T3 uses low-density freestanding edgeyard buildings.

q: Which frontage keeps the front yard unfenced and visually continuous with adjacent yards?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 51 — Frontage Types / Wind Exposure Category
n: A Common Lawn frontage leaves the front yard unfenced and visually continuous with neighboring yards.

q: Which Washington-pattern problem concerns intersections?
o: Intersections are too few for through traffic
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 50 — Street Pattern Types / Criteria For Responsive Environments
n: Washington’s diagonal intersections can be spatially ill-defined.

q: Which zone is limited to high-density attached courtyard and rearyard buildings?
ref: Principles of Planning Tables, p. 49 — Neighborhood Structure and Elements
n: T6 uses only high-density attached courtyard and rearyard types.
